businesses.pitch: A friendly centre where tutors help children get better at maths, reading and science.
businesses.earns: Parents pay for each lesson, and one tutor can teach a small group of children at the same time.
businesses.costs: Tutors' pay, rent for the rooms, books and worksheets, plus heating and electricity.
businesses.risks: A great tutor leaving, quiet school holidays, and parents walking away if their child stops improving.
businesses.tip: Show parents how their child is improving: happy parents tell other parents, and that's free advertising.

cases.title: Your first tutor
cases.story: Your centre opens on Monday and you need a tutor. Mrs Adeyemi, a trained teacher, asks $20 an hour. Jake, a student, asks $9. Every adult who works with children must pass a safety check, and Jake's will take two weeks.

options.text: Run a free taster lesson so parents can see the centre
options.result: Twelve families come to try a lesson. Eight of them sign up for the whole term.
options.lesson: Letting people try first is a great way to win their trust.

options.text: Promise parents that every child will get top marks
options.result: Lots of families sign up, but not every child gets top marks. Disappointed parents leave and tell their friends.
options.lesson: Promise only what you can deliver, then try to do even better.

options.text: Let Jake start on Monday, before his safety check comes back
options.result: A parent asks to see Jake's safety check. There isn't one yet, so families leave and you are fined for breaking the rules.
options.lesson: Safety rules protect children. Never skip them to save time.

options.text: Pay for an advert in the school newsletter
options.result: A few parents ring after seeing the advert. It helps, but most still want to see the centre first.
options.lesson: Adverts get attention, but trust is what makes people buy.

options.text: Hire Mrs Adeyemi, a trained teacher, at a fair $20 an hour
options.result: Parents love her calm lessons and clear progress notes. By the end of the month, every group is full.
options.lesson: Paying fairly for real skill brings customers who stay.

cases.title: Your best tutor might leave
cases.story: Sam is your most popular tutor. Another centre has offered him $3 more an hour, and he's thinking of leaving. Twelve families come especially for his lessons.

options.text: Make every tutor promise never to work for another centre
options.result: The tutors feel trapped and grumpy. Two of them start looking for new jobs.
options.lesson: People stay because they want to, not because they're forced to.

options.text: Raise Sam's pay by $2 and let him run a new science club
options.result: Sam stays and loves running the science club. Six new families join just to try it.
options.lesson: Keeping a great person is usually cheaper than replacing them.

options.text: Ask all your tutors what they enjoy and what they'd change
options.result: They ask for better books and a proper break room. Small changes, big smiles: nobody wants to leave now.
options.lesson: Asking your team what they need costs little and stops problems early.

options.text: Ask Sam to write down his best lesson ideas for the team
options.result: Now every tutor can use Sam's fun maths games. If he ever leaves, his ideas won't leave with him.
options.lesson: Don't let all your know-how live in one person's head.

cases.title: Test time rush
cases.story: Big tests are six weeks away. Forty new families want lessons, but you only have room for twenty. Then a man emails offering a copy of the real test answers for $300.

options.text: Squeeze ten children into every group
options.result: The rooms are noisy and crowded. Children get less help, and some parents complain and leave.
options.lesson: Cramming in more customers can spoil the very thing they came for.

options.text: Add Saturday classes and hire another safety-checked tutor
options.result: The Saturday groups fill up in two days. More children get help, and your income jumps.
options.lesson: When demand is bigger than you, grow carefully: more hours and more good people.

options.text: Start a waiting list and offer the next free places first
options.result: Families are happy to wait for a centre they trust. Your list is full until next term.
options.lesson: A waiting list keeps eager customers for later.

options.text: Raise prices a little for new families only
options.result: A few families say no, but most happily pay. You earn a bit more without upsetting your regulars.
options.lesson: When lots of people want what you sell, a small price rise can be fair.

options.text: Buy the secret test answers so every child gets top marks
options.result: The school finds out the answers were stolen. The test is cancelled, and furious parents blame you and want their money back.
options.lesson: Cheating breaks trust in a moment; real learning is what parents pay for.

businesses.pitch: A barber shop with two chairs, where people come for a haircut and a friendly chat.
businesses.earns: Each haircut costs $15. Regulars come back every few weeks, so a busy chair earns money all month long.
businesses.costs: Rent for the shop, the barbers' pay, clippers, towels, shampoo and the electricity bill.
businesses.risks: A cheaper barber nearby, a bad review online, or a great barber leaving and taking customers along.
businesses.tip: Remember names and how people like their hair: regulars who feel at home come back for years.

cases.title: Opening the doors
cases.story: Your shop has two chairs. You cut hair yourself and need one more barber. Most barbers nearby charge $15 for a cut. What will you do first?

options.text: Hire Tomas, a skilled barber, on fair pay plus his tips
options.result: Tomas is quick, friendly and brilliant with tricky haircuts. Customers start asking for him by name.
options.lesson: A skilled, fairly paid team member is the best advert a shop can have.

options.text: Give free haircuts to everyone for the whole first month
options.result: Crowds come for free cuts, but many never return once you charge. You worked a whole month for nothing.
options.lesson: Giving everything away attracts bargain hunters, not loyal customers.

options.text: Start a loyalty card: every sixth haircut is free
options.result: Customers love collecting stamps. Most come back every month to fill their cards.
options.lesson: Rewarding regulars keeps them coming to you, not to the shop down the road.

options.text: Charge $15 like everyone else, and $10 for children on weekdays
options.result: Parents bring children after school on quiet weekdays. Your chairs are busy even on Tuesdays.
options.lesson: A cheaper price at quiet times fills empty chairs without lowering your main price.

cases.title: A cheaper rival opens
cases.story: 'Quick Cuts' opens across the road, charging $8 a cut, and some of your customers try it. A website offers to sell you 200 five-star reviews for $300.

options.text: Add a free hot-towel finish and easy online booking
options.result: Customers notice the difference. Many who tried Quick Cuts come back, saying your cuts last longer.
options.lesson: You don't have to be the cheapest; be the one that's worth paying for.

options.text: Cut your price to $7 to beat them
options.result: The shop is packed, but each cut barely pays for itself. You're working harder for less money.
options.lesson: A price war with a cheaper rival usually makes you both poorer.

options.text: Ask happy customers to leave an honest review
options.result: Twenty real reviews appear, full of kind words about your barbers. New customers read them and come in.
options.lesson: Real reviews from happy customers are worth more than any advert.

options.text: Open late on Thursdays for people who work all day
options.result: Busy workers pop in after their jobs. Thursday evenings become your second-busiest time.
options.lesson: Opening when customers are free can win people a rival forgets about.

options.text: Pay $300 for 200 five-star reviews and look like the best shop
options.result: The review site spots the fakes, deletes them and puts a warning on your page. You are fined for tricking customers.
options.lesson: Fake reviews are lying to customers, and they nearly always get found out.

cases.title: Room to grow
cases.story: Your shop is full every Saturday and people wait an hour. The empty shop next door is for rent at $500 a month. The agent says: 'Three others want it. Sign the rent contract today!'

options.text: Sign the contract today, before the other people get it
options.result: The small print makes you pay for a new roof and stay for ten years. It's a huge bill you never saw coming.
options.lesson: 'Sign today or lose it!' is a pressure trick. A fair deal lets you read it first.

options.text: Text regulars to suggest quieter times, like Tuesday mornings
options.result: Many regulars are happy to come on quieter days. Saturdays are calmer, and Tuesdays get busier.
options.lesson: Spreading customers across the week can be cheaper than getting bigger.

options.text: Ask the agent for a lower rent and a shorter contract
options.result: The agent agrees to $450 a month for two years, not ten. Asking politely saves you $600 a year.
options.lesson: Asking for better terms costs nothing: the worst they can say is no.

options.text: Squeeze a third chair into your small shop
options.result: Barbers bump elbows and customers feel cramped. It's a little quicker, but nobody enjoys it.
options.lesson: Growing in a hurry can make a nice place feel worse.

options.text: Promote your best barber to run the new shop, with a pay rise
options.result: Your barber is proud to run the new shop. Saturday queues vanish, and both shops are busy.
options.lesson: Growing works best when you trust good people with real responsibility.

businesses.pitch: A bright parlour selling scoops, sundaes and milkshakes in lots of flavours.
businesses.earns: A scoop costs about 40 cents to make and sells for $3. On a hot day, hundreds of scoops go out of the door.
businesses.costs: Milk, cream and fruit, big freezers that use lots of electricity, staff pay and the shop's rent.
businesses.risks: Cold, rainy summers, empty winters, and a freezer breaking down with all the stock inside.
businesses.tip: Save money from the hot months for the winter bills, and give people a reason to visit when it's cold.

cases.title: Opening the parlour
cases.story: It's April, and your parlour opens next week. A scoop costs you about 40 cents to make and sells for $3. Summer is when you'll sell the most, so the first weeks really matter.

options.text: Give away free scoops every day for a whole month
options.result: Huge queues for free ice cream, but most people never buy once it costs money. You gave away $1,200 of stock.
options.lesson: Free treats should bring customers back, not just give your stock away.

options.text: Hire two cheerful part-time helpers for summer weekends
options.result: Weekend queues move quickly and nobody gives up waiting. Your helpers are great with families.
options.lesson: Extra hands at your busiest times turn long queues into sales.

options.text: Hold a 'name our new flavour' competition for local children
options.result: Over 200 names arrive. The winner, Strawberry Volcano, becomes your bestseller.
options.lesson: When customers help create something, they feel it's partly theirs.

options.text: Make your own ice cream with fresh milk from the local dairy
options.result: The fresh, creamy taste gets people talking. Queues form on the very first sunny Saturday.
options.lesson: A product people can't get anywhere else is worth a little extra cost.

cases.title: The freezer breaks
cases.story: On the hottest Saturday of the year, your biggest freezer breaks down. $1,200 of ice cream starts to melt, and the repair firm can't come until Monday.

options.text: Pay $1,200 for an emergency repair on Saturday night
options.result: The freezer works again by Sunday, but the repair cost as much as all the ice cream you saved.
options.lesson: Before paying to fix a problem, check the fix doesn't cost more than the problem.

options.text: Buy insurance that pays for spoiled stock in future
options.result: The next time something breaks, the insurance pays for the lost stock. You sleep better all summer.
options.lesson: Insurance costs a little each year to save you from a big loss one day.

options.text: Ask the café next door to keep your tubs in their freezer
options.result: Mrs Chen says yes if you send her some sundaes. Your stock is saved, and you've made a good friend.
options.lesson: Good neighbours are a business's secret safety net.

options.text: Sell the softest tubs today as $2 milkshakes
options.result: Milkshake fans queue up all afternoon, and very little ice cream goes to waste.
options.lesson: Quick thinking can turn a problem into a sale.

options.text: Refreeze the melted ice cream and sell it next week
options.result: Several customers get tummy aches. A food inspector closes the parlour for a week and fines you.
options.lesson: Never bend food safety rules: melted ice cream must not be refrozen.

cases.title: Winter is coming
cases.story: Summer is over, and ice cream sales drop by three quarters, but the $800 rent stays the same. A man offers you $3,000 for half of your parlour, forever, if you say yes tonight.

options.text: Take orders for ice cream birthday cakes all year round
options.result: Parents order cakes for winter birthdays. One cake earns as much as ten scoops.
options.lesson: Birthdays happen all year, so selling for them keeps money coming in.

options.text: Stay open until 10 pm every night to catch a few more customers
options.result: Night after night the shop sits empty, with the lights and freezers humming. The bills go up, not the sales.
options.lesson: Opening longer only helps if customers actually come.

options.text: Add hot waffles and hot chocolate to the winter menu
options.result: Warm waffles and hot chocolate bring families in on chilly days. Winter is no longer empty.
options.lesson: A second product for the quiet season smooths out the ups and downs.

options.text: Sell half the parlour tonight for $3,000
options.result: You get $3,000 now, but from next summer half of every scoop's profit goes to him, year after year.
options.lesson: Never sell part of your business in a hurry: a share is worth years of profit.

options.text: Use money saved in summer to pay the winter bills
options.result: Your summer savings cover the rent. No panic, no borrowing, and your staff still get paid.
options.lesson: Busy months should pay for quiet months: keep a cash cushion.

businesses.pitch: A warm bakery selling fresh bread, croissants and birthday cakes every morning.
businesses.earns: A loaf costs about $1 to make and sells for $3. Early customers buy bread, and party cakes earn extra.
businesses.costs: Flour, butter and eggs, gas for the ovens, the bakers' pay, and the shop's rent.
businesses.risks: Bread left over at closing time, flour prices going up, and a supermarket selling cheaper loaves.
businesses.tip: Bake to match what really sells: write down what's left each day and bake a little less of it tomorrow.

cases.title: Getting ready to bake
cases.story: Your ovens are ready. Mill Lane Flour sells good flour at $30 a sack and delivers every week. A website you've never heard of offers 'the same flour' for $10 a sack, if you pay for a whole year up front.

options.text: Label every cake that contains nuts, milk or eggs
options.result: A mum whose son has a nut allergy thanks you for the clear labels, and tells all her friends.
options.lesson: Clear allergy labels keep customers safe and earn their trust.

options.text: Buy from Mill Lane and ask for a regular-order discount
options.result: Mill Lane agrees to $27 a sack for a weekly order. Your bread tastes great, and your costs are lower.
options.lesson: A reliable supplier plus a polite request for a discount is a winning recipe.

options.text: Hand out warm bread samples at the door in opening week
options.result: The smell of warm bread pulls people in. Many become regulars who come every morning.
options.lesson: Let your best product sell itself: a free taste can win a customer for years.

options.text: Sell loaves for $1.20 to beat the supermarket
options.result: You're busy all day but make almost nothing on each loaf. One slow week and you can't pay the rent.
options.lesson: A price must cover your costs and leave a profit, or being busy just makes it worse.

options.text: Pay the new website a year up front for $10 flour
options.result: The website takes your $1,350 and vanishes. No flour ever comes, so you rush to buy more at full price.
options.lesson: Unknown, super cheap and 'pay everything first' are the warning signs of a scam.

cases.title: Too much bread left over
cases.story: Every evening, about 20 loaves are left unsold. That's around $600 a month of flour, butter and hard work going in the bin.

options.text: Sell yesterday's bread tomorrow as 'baked this morning'
options.result: Customers notice the stale crusts. One complains to the council, you are fined, and regulars stop trusting your sign.
options.lesson: Calling old food fresh is lying, and lost trust is hard to win back.

options.text: Sell what's left at half price in the last hour
options.result: Bargain hunters queue at five o'clock. Almost nothing goes in the bin any more.
options.lesson: Half price is better than no price for food that won't keep.

options.text: Give leftover loaves to the local food bank
options.result: The food bank is so grateful, and the local paper writes about your kindness. More people choose your shop.
options.lesson: Helping your community is the right thing to do, and people remember it.

options.text: Keep a daily record: bake more of what sells out, less of what doesn't
options.result: Your notebook shows white loaves sell out but seeded ones don't. Swapping trays cuts waste and sells more.
options.lesson: Your sales records tell you what to bake: let the numbers guide the oven.

cases.title: A big café order
cases.story: A café chain wants 100 croissants a week at $1 each. They'd pay 60 days after each delivery, so you'd buy butter and flour for two months before any money arrives.

options.text: Say yes, but ask to be paid every two weeks instead
options.result: The café agrees to pay every two weeks. Money comes in steadily, and your bakery hums along.
options.lesson: A big order is only good if the money arrives in time to pay your own bills.

options.text: Start with a one-month trial to see if it works for you both
options.result: The trial shows you can bake them easily before opening time. Both sides happily carry on.
options.lesson: A small trial lets you test a big deal before you bet on it.

options.text: Hire a part-time baker for the early croissant shift
options.result: Amara joins at 5 am, three days a week. The croissants are ready on time, and you get some sleep.
options.lesson: When you grow, get help early, before you wear yourself out.

options.text: Swap butter for cheap margarine to earn more on each one
options.result: The café notices the croissants taste greasy and stops the order after a month.
options.lesson: Cutting quality to squeeze out profit can lose you the customer altogether.

businesses.pitch: A friendly pet shop selling fish, pet food, toys and cosy beds for cats and dogs.
businesses.earns: Owners buy pet food every week or two, and toys, tanks and treats add extra, especially at Christmas.
businesses.costs: Stock from suppliers, the shop's rent, staff pay, and heating and filters for the fish tanks.
businesses.risks: Online pet stores selling cheaper, food going out of date, and sick fish if the tanks aren't cared for.
businesses.tip: Give owners good advice and help them care for their pets: they'll trust you and buy from you for years.

cases.title: Filling the shelves
cases.story: Your shelves are empty. A trusted supplier sells Happy Paws dog food at $20 a bag, and you can sell it for $28. A man in a van offers 'Happy Paws' bags for $8 each, cash only, no receipt.

options.text: Fill the shop with 30 kinds of fish to look impressive
options.result: Caring for so many tanks is hard work. Some fish get sick, and you can't sell them.
options.lesson: Start with what customers ask for, not with everything you could buy.

options.text: Buy from the trusted supplier, starting with what owners ask for
options.result: You stock the foods local owners ask for most. They sell fast, and nothing sits on the shelf for long.
options.lesson: Stock what your customers actually want, from suppliers you can trust.

options.text: Offer free nail trims for dogs on Saturday mornings
options.result: Dog owners queue up on Saturdays, and most buy food or treats while they wait.
options.lesson: A small free service brings people through the door, and they rarely leave empty-handed.

options.text: Hire Ana, who studied animal care, to give owners advice
options.result: Ana helps a girl choose the right food for her old cat. Her family now buys everything from you.
options.lesson: Expert advice turns a quick visit into a loyal customer.

options.text: Buy the $8 'Happy Paws' bags from the van for a huge profit
options.result: The food is fake and upsets several dogs' tummies. You refund the owners, pay the vet bills and lose their trust.
options.lesson: A famous brand at a third of the price, cash only, is almost always a fake.

cases.title: The giant online store
cases.story: PetMegaStore online now sells dog food $3 cheaper than you, with free delivery. Some of your regulars have stopped coming in.

options.text: Let regulars order online and get local delivery
options.result: Busy owners love having heavy bags brought to their door. Many come back to you.
options.lesson: Meet customers where they are, even if that's on their phone.

options.text: Match their price on your five best-selling foods
options.result: Regulars notice the fair prices and return. You earn a little less per bag, but you keep them as customers.
options.lesson: Matching price on your key products can stop customers drifting away.

options.text: Offer what a website can't: expert advice and a puppy class
options.result: Your Saturday puppy class is a hit. Owners stay to chat, ask questions and buy their food while they're here.
options.lesson: Don't fight a giant on price; win on the things only you can do.

options.text: Tell customers the website's food is old (you don't know that)
options.result: A customer checks, and it isn't true. Word gets round that you tell fibs, and people trust your advice less.
options.lesson: Spreading rumours about a rival makes you look worse, not them.

cases.title: The Christmas rush
cases.story: December is your busiest month. A supplier offers 400 pet Christmas stockings at $2 each, if you buy them all today. Some parents want to buy rabbits as surprise presents.

options.text: Make a festive window of gift bundles from your shelves
options.result: Your twinkly window of treats and toys stops shoppers in the street. December sales are your best ever.
options.lesson: A great window display is an advert that works all day long.

options.text: Hire a cheerful helper for the busy December weekends
options.result: With an extra pair of hands, nobody waits long. Shoppers leave smiling with bags full of presents.
options.lesson: Extra help at your busiest time keeps customers happy and sales flowing.

options.text: Sell rabbits as surprise presents to anyone who asks
options.result: In January, several rabbits are brought back by families who weren't ready. The local paper isn't kind.
options.lesson: Selling a pet to someone who isn't ready is bad for the pet and for your name.

options.text: Sell gift vouchers so families can choose a pet together later
options.result: Vouchers sell well, and in January families come in calm and ready. The new pets go to happy, prepared homes.
options.lesson: A pet is for life, not just for Christmas: help families get it right.

options.text: Buy all 400 stockings today to get the low price
options.result: You sell 120. The other 280 sit in the stockroom until next Christmas, taking up space.
options.lesson: A bargain is only a bargain if you can sell it in time.

businesses.pitch: A shop that prints posters, leaflets and T-shirts, and designs logos for local people.
businesses.earns: Customers pay for each job: 500 leaflets might cost $15 to print and sell for $60. Schools and clubs order again and again.
businesses.costs: Big printers, ink and paper, a designer's pay, and the shop's rent.
businesses.risks: A printer breaking at a busy time, customers who pay late, and cheap printing websites.
businesses.tip: Always show customers a proof, one test copy, before printing 1,000 of anything: mistakes are expensive.

cases.title: Setting up shop
cases.story: You open in September, when schools and clubs need posters and programmes. The big colour printer costs $4,200 to buy, or $150 a month to rent with repairs included.

options.text: Skip showing customers a test copy so jobs get done faster
options.result: A school programme comes back with the head teacher's name spelt wrong. You reprint 300 copies for free.
options.lesson: Checking a test copy takes minutes; reprinting takes hours and money.

options.text: Download a free copy of a $600 design program from a random site
options.result: The 'free' program hides a virus that locks your computer. Customers' files are lost, and the expert fix costs a fortune.
options.lesson: 'Free' copies of paid software are stolen, and they often carry viruses.

options.text: Hire a part-time designer to make customers' ideas look great
options.result: Priya turns scribbled ideas into beautiful posters. Customers come back just for her designs.
options.lesson: Skilled people can turn a simple service into something special.

options.text: Rent the printer with repairs included, and keep your cash
options.result: When the printer jams in October, it's fixed free the next day. Your $4,200 stays safe in the bank.
options.lesson: Renting can beat buying when it keeps your cash free and the repairs covered.

options.text: Visit five local schools with free sample posters
options.result: Three schools love your samples and order programmes for their autumn concerts. One asks for a new logo too.
options.lesson: Go and show customers what you can do, instead of waiting for them to find you.

cases.title: Breakdown before the deadline
cases.story: The day before twenty orders are due, your big printer jams and won't start. The repair person can't come until the day after tomorrow, and customers are counting on you.

options.text: Phone every customer, explain, and offer a new time with 10% off
options.result: Most customers thank you for telling them early. Only two need their jobs today, and you sort those out.
options.lesson: Telling customers about a problem early keeps their trust, even when things go wrong.

options.text: Buy a small back-up printer for emergencies
options.result: The little printer can't do big posters, but it handles leaflets whenever the big one is down.
options.lesson: A back-up plan seems a waste until the day you need it.

options.text: Pay a print shop across town to do the most urgent jobs
options.result: The other shop prints your urgent jobs overnight. You earn a little less, but every deadline is met.
options.lesson: Even a rival can be a helpful partner in an emergency.

options.text: Print the jobs on your blotchy old office printer anyway
options.result: Faint, streaky posters go out of the door. Two clubs ask for their money back.
options.lesson: Rushing out poor work hurts your name more than being a little late.

cases.title: 1,000 football shirts
cases.story: A man wants 1,000 T-shirts printed with a famous football club's badge, to sell outside the stadium. He'll pay $5,000 cash today. He hasn't got the club's permission, but says 'nobody checks'.

options.text: Offer to design him an original fan shirt with no club badge
options.result: He likes your fun original design. The shirts sell well, and he comes back for scarves and hats.
options.lesson: When a deal is wrong, look for an honest version that still works for everyone.

options.text: Print the shirts: $5,000 cash is a lot of money!
options.result: The club finds the fake shirts and traces them to you. The shirts are taken away, and you pay a big fine.
options.lesson: Printing someone else's badge without permission is making fakes, and that's against the law.

options.text: Advertise custom shirts to local sports teams and schools
options.result: Junior football and netball teams order shirts with their own badges. It's steady work you're proud of.
options.lesson: There's plenty of honest work if you go looking for it.

options.text: Say no politely, and explain the badge belongs to the club
options.result: He shrugs and leaves. Weeks later you hear his fake shirts were taken away from another printer, who was fined.
options.lesson: Saying no to a dishonest deal protects your business and your name.

businesses.pitch: A taco truck that drives to wherever the hungry crowds are.
businesses.earns: Each taco costs about $1 to make and sells for $4. A busy lunchtime or a summer festival can sell hundreds.
businesses.costs: Ingredients, fuel, fees for good spots to park, the cook's pay, and keeping the truck on the road.
businesses.risks: Rainy days, a breakdown on the way to a big event, and a food inspection you're not ready for.
businesses.tip: Follow the crowds, and post where you'll be each day so your fans can find you.

cases.title: Where to park?
cases.story: Your taco truck is ready to roll. Office workers want lunch on Park Road, but a council permit to sell there costs $750. Outside the busy station there's no fee, but parking isn't allowed.

options.text: Post your weekly route online so fans can find you
options.result: Fans start following your truck online. Some even cross town for your Friday fish tacos.
options.lesson: Telling customers where you'll be turns one-time buyers into fans.

options.text: Park outside the busy station: no fee to pay!
options.result: Buses can't get past. You're fined twice, and on Friday the truck is towed away. That cost far more than the permit!
options.lesson: Breaking parking rules to save a fee usually ends up costing more.

options.text: Pay $750 for the Park Road permit and serve office lunches
options.result: Office workers queue every lunchtime. The permit pays for itself in the first two weeks.
options.lesson: Paying for the right spot is an investment when the customers are there.

options.text: Charge just $2 a taco to get huge crowds
options.result: The queues are long, but each taco barely covers its cost. Busy days leave you tired and no richer.
options.lesson: Low prices bring crowds, but only a fair profit on each one pays the bills.

options.text: Keep the menu small: three tacos done brilliantly
options.result: Food comes out fast, nothing goes to waste, and people rave about your three tacos.
options.lesson: Doing a few things brilliantly beats doing lots of things badly.

cases.title: The food inspector
cases.story: A food inspector visits on Friday. Her score for cleanliness and safety will be shown to customers. Your fridge has been running a bit warm, and you haven't written down its temperature every day like you should.

options.text: Close the truck on Friday so the inspector can't visit
options.result: The inspector simply comes back next week, extra careful. You lost a busy day of sales for nothing.
options.lesson: Hiding from a problem doesn't make it go away.

options.text: Fill in a week of pretend temperatures before Friday
options.result: The inspector's thermometer shows the fridge is too warm, so your log is clearly made up. You're fined and get one star out of five.
options.lesson: Faking safety records is dishonest and dangerous, and inspectors know the signs.

options.text: Ask a friend who runs a café to look over your truck first
options.result: She spots a greasy fan above the cooker that you'd stopped noticing. It's cleaned before Friday.
options.lesson: A fresh pair of experienced eyes can spot what you've stopped seeing.

options.text: Send your cook on a short food safety course
options.result: Your cook comes back full of good habits: clean boards, hot food hot, cold food cold.
options.lesson: Training your team means good habits happen even when you're not watching.

options.text: Fix the fridge now and start a daily temperature log
options.result: The inspector checks your fridge and your new log, and gives you five stars. You proudly stick it on the window.
options.lesson: Doing safety properly every day means inspections are nothing to fear.

cases.title: The summer festival
cases.story: The Summer Music Festival wants your truck for three days, and 5,000 hungry people are expected. The organisers pay you a $1,000 deposit in cash today to save your place.

options.text: Bring ten kinds of taco so everyone finds one they like
options.result: Service is slow, the truck is a mess, and lots of ingredients go to waste in the heat.
options.lesson: At a busy event, a simple menu is faster and wastes less.

options.text: Team up with a lemonade stall to share a pitch and a queue
options.result: Tacos and lemonade go together perfectly. Customers buy both, and you each sell more.
options.lesson: The right partner can help you both win.

options.text: Hire and train a helper so the queue moves fast
options.result: With two of you serving, the queue never gets too long. Happy festival-goers come back for seconds.
options.lesson: Long queues lose sales; the right helper wins them back.

options.text: Keep the $1,000 cash deposit secret so you pay less tax
options.result: The festival's records show they paid you. The tax office finds the missing $1,000, and you pay a big fine on top.
options.lesson: Every dollar a business takes belongs in its accounts; hiding money is against the law.

options.text: Ask the organisers what sold last year, then plan your stock
options.result: Last year people wanted quick, simple food. You prepare plenty of easy tacos and sell out on the last night, with no waste.
options.lesson: Planning with real numbers means more sales and less waste.

businesses.pitch: A bright launderette where people wash and dry their clothes, or pay you to do it.
businesses.earns: Customers pay $4 a wash and $2 a dry. A service wash, where your staff do it all, costs more and earns more.
businesses.costs: Water, electricity, soap, machine repairs, the attendant's pay and the shop's rent.
businesses.risks: Machines breaking down, a burst pipe flooding the floor, and customers upset about damaged clothes.
businesses.tip: Machines that always work and a shop that's always clean bring people back every single week.

cases.title: Opening the launderette
cases.story: Ten new washing machines arrive next week, and the $6,000 bill is due. Then an email arrives that looks like it's from the machine company: 'We've changed banks. Please pay to this new account today.'

options.text: Give a free first wash to people in the flats nearby
options.result: Lots of neighbours try a free wash, and many of them come back every week after that.
options.lesson: A free first try is a good way to turn neighbours into regulars.

options.text: Pay the new account today so the machines arrive on time
options.result: The machine company never gets the money. A scammer has your $6,000, and you still owe the real bill.
options.lesson: An email asking you to pay a new account is a classic trick: check before you pay.

options.text: Hire a friendly attendant and offer a 'we wash it for you' service
options.result: Mr Osei keeps the shop spotless and does service washes for busy families. Each one earns twice as much as a normal wash.
options.lesson: A friendly face and an extra service can make an ordinary shop special.

options.text: Phone the machine company on the number you already have
options.result: They never sent that email! It came from a scammer. You pay the real account and warn the company.
options.lesson: Always check changed bank details by phoning a number you already trust.

options.text: Stay open all night with nobody looking after the shop
options.result: At night, machines get jammed and nobody tidies up. In the morning, your regulars walk into a mess.
options.lesson: Opening longer only helps if you can keep the place safe and clean.

cases.title: A shrunken jumper
cases.story: Mrs Kowalski is upset. Her favourite wool jumper shrank in your service wash, and she's written a one-star review: 'They ruined my clothes!' The jumper cost $60.

options.text: Get insurance that pays if customers' clothes are damaged
options.result: The next time something goes wrong, the insurance pays the customer quickly. Nobody has to argue.
options.lesson: Insurance turns a scary surprise into a small, planned cost.

options.text: Train staff to check every label and wash wool on a cool setting
options.result: Now every bag is sorted by its labels. Months go by without a single shrunken jumper.
options.lesson: Fix the cause of a mistake, not just the mistake itself.

options.text: Put up a sign: 'We are not responsible for damaged clothes'
options.result: Customers read the sign and frown. Some take their washing to the launderette across town.
options.lesson: A sign that dodges blame tells customers you won't look after them.

options.text: Say sorry, pay for the jumper, and reply kindly to her review
options.result: Mrs Kowalski is surprised and pleased. She changes her review: 'Mistakes happen, but they made it right!'
options.lesson: How you fix a mistake can win more trust than never making one.

cases.title: The hotel's big order
cases.story: The Grand Hotel wants you to wash 300 sheets a week for $900 a month. In the day your machines are busy, but at night they stand empty. The contract is ten pages long.

options.text: Wash the hotel's sheets at night, when the machines stand empty
options.result: Your night-time washing hums along while the town sleeps. Daytime customers never notice, and your income jumps.
options.lesson: Using machines that would sit idle is one of the smartest ways to grow.

options.text: Work out what 300 sheets really cost you before agreeing a price
options.result: Your sums show $900 barely covers soap and power. You ask for $1,100, and the hotel agrees.
options.lesson: Know your costs before you name your price.

options.text: Read all ten pages carefully before you sign
options.result: Page nine says you pay $200 for every late bag. You ask them to change it, and they do.
options.lesson: The small print is where the costly surprises hide.

options.text: Borrow money to buy five more machines straight away
options.result: The new machines mostly stand still, but the loan payments arrive every single month.
options.lesson: Use what you already have before you borrow to buy more.

businesses.pitch: A busy gym with weights, running machines and fun fitness classes for grown-ups and teens.
businesses.earns: Members pay $30 a month. With 200 members, that's $6,000 a month coming in before costs.
businesses.costs: Rent for a big space, trainers' pay, electricity, showers and towels, and fixing the machines.
businesses.risks: Members who stop coming after January, a cheaper gym nearby, and injuries if equipment isn't safe.
businesses.tip: Members who make friends at the gym keep coming: classes and friendly trainers matter more than shiny machines.

cases.title: Opening in January
cases.story: Your gym opens in January, when lots of people want to get fit. Most gyms nearby charge $30 a month, plus a $50 joining fee. How will you win your first members?

options.text: Drop the joining fee for everyone who joins in January
options.result: With no joining fee, 150 people sign up in January. It's a flying start.
options.lesson: Removing a small barrier at the right moment can bring a rush of customers.

options.text: Hire two friendly trainers to run free beginner classes
options.result: Nervous beginners love the friendly classes. Many say they'd never have joined a gym otherwise.
options.lesson: Make new customers feel welcome and they'll keep coming.

options.text: Give local office workers a free two-week trial
options.result: Lots of office workers try it at lunchtime, and a good number sign up when the trial ends.
options.lesson: A free trial lets people discover they like you.

options.text: Charge just $10 a month to fill the gym fast
options.result: The gym is packed and the machines keep breaking, but $10 doesn't cover the costs. You lose money every month.
options.lesson: Cheap prices that don't cover costs fill the room and empty the bank.

options.text: Hide extra fees in the small print for more money each month
options.result: Members feel tricked when surprise fees appear. Angry reviews pour in, and you must refund many of them.
options.lesson: Tricking customers with small print wins money once and loses trust for good.

cases.title: The February fade
cases.story: In January, 150 new members joined. Now it's February, and half of them have stopped coming. People who never come usually cancel soon after.

options.text: Give each new member a free session to plan their goals
options.result: With a clear plan, new members see progress and keep coming. Trainers get to know them by name.
options.lesson: Customers who reach their goals stay, so help them get there.

options.text: Start a gym buddy club and fun group classes
options.result: Members who train with a buddy keep turning up. By March, most of them are still coming, and loving it.
options.lesson: People stick with things they enjoy doing with friends.

options.text: Make cancelling hard: only in person, on Monday mornings
options.result: Members get cross and write angry reviews. People read them and choose a different gym.
options.lesson: Making it hard to leave just makes people want to leave more.

options.text: Spend $4,500 on big adverts to replace them
options.result: New people join in March, then stop coming in April, just like the others.
options.lesson: Keeping the customers you have is cheaper than always finding new ones.

options.text: Send a friendly message to members who've stopped coming
options.result: 'We miss you!' messages bring dozens back. Some just needed a little nudge.
options.lesson: A friendly reminder can win back customers who were drifting away.

cases.title: Miracle Muscle pills
cases.story: A man named Rick wants to be your partner: 'Sell my Miracle Muscle pills at your front desk. Muscles in one week! You'll make $3,000 a month.' The pills have no safety label.

options.text: Ask your trainers what members really want to buy
options.result: The trainers suggest water bottles, gym towels and yoga mats. They all sell steadily.
options.lesson: The people closest to customers often have the best product ideas.

options.text: Partner with Rick: $3,000 a month for doing nothing!
options.result: Some members feel ill after taking the pills. The pills are banned, you are fined, and the local news names your gym.
options.lesson: Big promises, easy money and no safety label: that's a get-rich-quick trap.

options.text: Hold a free healthy-eating talk with a real nutrition expert
options.result: Members learn that good food, sleep and training build muscle. They trust your gym even more.
options.lesson: Honest advice builds trust that no magic pill can buy.

options.text: Open a smoothie bar with healthy snacks instead
options.result: After a workout, members love a banana smoothie. The bar earns money every day, and it's honest.
options.lesson: Sell things that truly help your customers, and they'll keep buying.

businesses.pitch: A building of eight flats where tenants pay you rent every month to live there.
businesses.earns: Eight tenants each pay $350 a month in rent. That's $2,800 coming in before repairs and other costs.
businesses.costs: Repairs, insurance, cleaning the stairs, safety checks, and saving for big jobs like a new roof.
businesses.risks: Empty flats with no rent coming in, a tenant who can't pay, and costly repairs like a leaking roof.
businesses.tip: Treat tenants fairly and fix things fast: happy tenants stay for years and look after your building.

cases.title: Getting the flats ready
cases.story: You now own a block of eight flats, and twenty people want to rent one. Rents nearby are $350 a month. Each tenant pays a $700 deposit: money you look after in case of damage. By law it must be kept in a special safe scheme.

options.text: Buy landlord insurance against fire, floods and storms
options.result: You hope you'll never need it, but if a storm hits, the insurance will help pay for the repairs.
options.lesson: Insurance protects the thing you worked so hard to buy.

options.text: Fit smoke alarms and get the gas checked before anyone moves in
options.result: Every flat passes its safety checks. Tenants move in feeling safe, and they tell friends about their caring landlord.
options.lesson: A landlord's first job is keeping tenants safe in their homes.

options.text: Charge $500 a month: somebody might pay it
options.result: Only three flats fill. The others stay empty for months, so you earn less than you would at a fair rent.
options.lesson: A fair rent keeps your flats full; empty flats earn nothing.

options.text: Keep the deposits in your own account and spend them on repairs
options.result: When tenants move out, there's no deposit to give back. A court orders you to pay each of them three times as much.
options.lesson: Money you hold for someone else isn't yours to spend.

options.text: Ask every renter the same questions, and check with their old landlord
options.result: Treating everyone the same, you choose tenants who are honest and can afford the rent. Rent arrives on time.
options.lesson: Fair, careful checks find good tenants and treat everyone equally.

cases.title: A tenant can't pay
cases.story: Mrs Okafor has lived in Flat 3 for four years and always paid on time. She has lost her job and can't pay this month's $350 rent. She's looking hard for new work.

options.text: Keep a savings pot so one late rent doesn't hurt
options.result: This month your savings cover the gap. No panic, and the money for the roof stays safe.
options.lesson: Saving for bad months means one problem never becomes a disaster.

options.text: Agree a plan: she pays a little each week until she catches up
options.result: Mrs Okafor finds a new job in six weeks and pays back every dollar. She tells everyone you're the fairest landlord in town.
options.lesson: Being fair to a good tenant in a hard time pays you back in trust.

options.text: Help her find a free advice centre for money and jobs
options.result: The advice centre helps her get support while she looks for work. She's grateful you cared.
options.lesson: Pointing people to the right help is kind and practical.

options.text: Raise everyone's rent to cover her missing $350
options.result: The other tenants are cross about paying for something that isn't their fault. Two start looking for new flats.
options.lesson: Making other customers pay for one problem is unfair, and they notice.

options.text: Change the locks while she's out and rent the flat to someone else
options.result: That's against the law. A court orders you to let her back in and pay her for the trouble, and now every tenant distrusts you.
options.lesson: A landlord must follow the law, even when a tenant owes money.

cases.title: A leaky roof
cases.story: After a storm, rain drips into Flat 8. A trusted local builder can fix the roof next week for $9,000, with a 10-year guarantee. A man knocks on your door: 'I'll patch it today for $3,000 cash. No paperwork.'

options.text: Let the man at the door patch it today for $3,000 cash
options.result: He rushes the job and vanishes. In the next storm the leak is worse, and with no paperwork there's no way to find him.
options.lesson: Cash-only workers at the door give you no guarantee and no one to complain to.

options.text: Paint over the damp patch so it looks fine for now
options.result: Within a week the paint bubbles and the damp spreads. The family is upset you tried to hide it.
options.lesson: Covering up a problem doesn't fix it; it just makes it bigger.

options.text: Hire the trusted builder with the 10-year guarantee
options.result: The roof is fixed properly and stays dry through every storm after. The Flat 8 family is relieved and stays for years.
options.lesson: Paying for proper work once is cheaper than paying for bad work twice.

options.text: Check the other seven flats for storm damage too
options.result: You find a cracked window in Flat 2 and fix it before the next rain. A small fix saves a big bill.
options.lesson: After one problem, look for others while they're still small.

options.text: Pay for the Flat 8 family to stay somewhere dry until it's fixed
options.result: The family is grateful you looked after them. They come back to a dry flat and a landlord they trust.
options.lesson: Caring for tenants in a crisis builds loyalty money can't buy.
